c: Royal Psalms
The
royal psalms
all have some reference to the king, the nature of his rule, and his relationship to God.
are usually regarded as the royal psalms.
Belief in God’s kingship is the foundation of the royal psalms (see

). Each king in David’s dynasty served as messianic agent—i.e., he represented God’s kingship. As God’s representative, the Davidic king was expected to uphold the qualities of justice, righteousness, faithfulness, and peace (
The royal psalms express the hope and aspirations of the dynasty of David. But with its corruption and failure, the dynasty came to an apparent end (

). Yet hope remained alive for the future of a king descended from David who would serve as God’s agent. The royal psalms maintain this hope for a king whose perfect obedience would guarantee the continuity of David’s dynasty and the perpetual benefits of his reign.
In this sense, the royal psalms may also be called
messianic psalms
in that they express hope in a messianic agent, an ideal king descended from David. Jesus stated that the psalmists wrote of him (
), and other NT writers affirmed the identification of Jesus as the Messiah. Some of the most significant links to Christ are as follows:

Passages for Further Study
God’s Anger
The Lord is just and righteous in his judgment (
), and he experiences anger at sin and injustice. The wicked stir up his anger and deserve his judgment (see
; see also
). And while he is patient and slow to anger (
), he ultimately will not allow evil to remain unchecked.
The psalmists understood Israel’s exodus from Egypt as an object lesson about God’s anger. God expressed his anger against the Egyptians while sparing his people (
). But Israel itself became the object of God’s anger during the wilderness journey, when the people provoked the Lord through their rebelliousness (
). As a result, God took an oath: That rebellious generation would not enter his place of rest (
). So they died in the wilderness. But he restrained his anger and did not destroy Israel as they deserved (

). Similarly, throughout the period of the judges and the monarchy, God’s people were marked by disobedience and evil; subsequently, in his wrath, God allowed them to be controlled by foreign powers, who sent them into exile (
). But again, God did not allow his people to be completely destroyed.
When God’s people sin and experience his anger, it can precipitate repentance, in which case the experience, though painful, can lead to great joy in God’s mercy and goodness (
; see also
The New Testament makes clear that all of humanity was subject to God’s wrath on account of sin (
). But in his love, God sent his son, Jesus Christ, to atone for our sins and reconcile us to God (
). Those who turn to God in faith will thus escape the punishment that is coming at the future judgment of the world. In the end, Jesus will serve as the agent of God’s anger against the wicked (
), who—along with God’s ultimate enemy, the devil—will be dealt with decisively (
